title: Citizen Kane
events_chronological: In 1871 Colorado, Mrs. Kane signs her son Charles over to the banker Thatcher after a defaulted boarder's mine deed makes the family rich.
The boy drives his sled into Thatcher's stomach and is taken east away from his parents anyway.
On his twenty-fifth birthday Kane takes control of the fortune and tells Thatcher that of all his holdings he wants to run the New York Inquirer.
Kane moves into the Inquirer, installs Bernstein and Leland, and prints a Declaration of Principles on the front page.
Kane hires away the entire staff of the rival Chronicle and throws a party with a brass band and a chorus line.
Kane returns from a European buying trip engaged to Emily Norton, the President's niece.
A run of breakfast-table scenes charts the Kanes' marriage cooling into silence behind separate newspapers.
Kane meets the shopgirl Susan Alexander on the street with mud on his coat and starts visiting her flat in secret.
Mid-campaign for governor, Boss Gettys brings Emily to Susan's flat and threatens exposure, and Kane refuses to withdraw.
Kane loses the election, Leland asks to be transferred to Chicago, and the marriage collapses.
Kane marries Susan and forces her into an opera career for which she has no voice.
Susan's Chicago debut is a humiliation, and a drunk Leland begins the savage review that Kane finishes, prints, and fires him for.
Susan swallows poison rather than sing again, and Kane finally lets her stop.
Kane shuts Susan away in the half-finished Xanadu, where she works jigsaw puzzles in the vast empty hall.
After a joyless beach picnic and a quarrel, Susan packs and leaves him.
Kane wrecks Susan's bedroom, finds a glass snow globe, murmurs "Rosebud", and carries it past the endless mirrors.
Alone at Xanadu, Kane dies with the word "Rosebud" on his lips and drops the snow globe on the floor.
A "News on the March" newsreel recaps Kane's public life and closes without explaining his last word.
The reporter Thompson is sent to find out what "Rosebud" means and is turned away by a drunk Susan in an Atlantic City nightclub.

Thompson reads Thatcher's memoir and interviews Bernstein, Leland, Susan and the butler Raymond before concluding that no single word explains a life, as workmen shovel a sled marked Rosebud into the furnace.
syuzhet_notes: The film's present tense is only told-order bullets 1-3 and the last bullet - Kane's death and Thompson's investigation. Everything between is flashback, and the flashbacks are not one continuous line but five overlapping first-hand accounts (Thatcher's memoir, then Bernstein, Leland, Susan and Raymond). Told-order bullet 15 doubles back behind bullet 14 because Susan's account restarts earlier than Leland's had finished, retelling the opera years from her side.
fabula_notes: The sled's identity as Rosebud is withheld until the final shot and no character in the film ever learns it. Kane's years abroad and the collapse of his fortune in the Depression are summarised by the newsreel rather than dramatised, and Susan's account of the debut covers the same night Leland has already narrated.
